t: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: What MAVLink Is: The Vehicle's Language
title: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: What MAVLink Is: The Vehicle's Language
description: MAVLink (Micro Air Vehicle Link) is the lingua franca of small uncrewed vehicles: a lightweight binary protocol where the aircraft and ground station exchange messages — HEARTBEAT ('I am alive, this is my type and mode'), SYS_STATUS (battery, sensors), GLOBAL_POSITION_INT, and COMMAND_LONG for orders. Version 2 adds message signing and a bigger message space. It runs over serial, SiK radios, or IP; QGroundControl, PX4, and ArduPilot all speak it. Learn MAVLink and you can talk to nearly any drone.
key_facts: Binary protocol for vehicles and ground stations
v2 adds signing and bigger message space

t: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Message Anatomy: Framing and CRC
title: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Message Anatomy: Framing and CRC
description: A MAVLink v1 frame is: start byte 0xFE, length, sequence, system ID, component ID, message ID, payload, and a 2-byte X.25 CRC seeded per message type. The CRC is the integrity story — corrupted radio bytes are detected and dropped. Parsing is a state machine over the byte stream: find the start byte, read the header, accumulate payload, verify CRC. Every ground-station developer implements this parser once and never forgets it.
key_facts: STX, length, seq, sys/comp ID, msg ID, CRC

t: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Dialects: Common, ArduPilot, PX4
title: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Dialects: Common, ArduPilot, PX4
description: MAVLink dialects are XML message definitions: the common dialect has the shared messages, and autopilots extend it (ardupilotmega, PX4-specific). Code generators turn the XML into C, Python (pymavlink), and other libraries — the protocol is defined once, implemented everywhere. Dialect mismatch is the classic integration bug: the ground station must speak the dialect the vehicle expects, or messages go unrecognized.

t: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Heartbeat: The Link's Pulse
title: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Heartbeat: The Link's Pulse
description: HEARTBEAT is the protocol's pulse: broadcast at 1 Hz, it carries vehicle type, autopilot class, base mode, custom mode, and system status. Ground stations use it for discovery (a new heartbeat means a new vehicle), link-loss detection (no heartbeat for N seconds means the link is dead), and mode display. The failsafe logic of every ground station starts here: silence is the signal.
key_facts: 1 Hz broadcast of type, mode, status

t: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Telemetry Streams: Rates and Budgets
title: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Telemetry Streams: Rates and Budgets
description: MAVLink telemetry is budgeted: high-rate attitude (50 Hz) for the HUD, position at 10 Hz, battery at 1 Hz — each stream requested with SR parameters or message intervals. Radio links are narrow (SiK radios ~57 kbps), so the stream budget is real engineering: too much telemetry starves commands. The discipline is requesting what the mission needs and no more, with the critical streams (heartbeat, status) always protected.

t: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Commands: The COMMAND_LONG Pattern
title: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Commands: The COMMAND_LONG Pattern
description: Orders go as COMMAND_LONG: command ID plus seven parameters (e.g., MAV_CMD_NAV_TAKEOFF with altitude in param 7), acknowledged by COMMAND_ACK with success or failure. The ack closes the loop — no ack, no assumption. Long commands (missions, parameter sets) use the mission and parameter protocols with their own ack sequences. The professional habit is verifying the ack and the resulting state, not just sending the command.

t: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Defensive Uses: Auditable Vehicle Links
title: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Defensive Uses: Auditable Vehicle Links
description: MAVLink's defensive value is openness with accountability: because the protocol is open, links can be monitored, logged, and audited — every command to the vehicle is a parseable message, not a proprietary secret. Signed v2 messages add authentication. Programs log all link traffic for post-mission review: who commanded what, when, and what the vehicle acknowledged. An auditable link is a trustworthy link.

t: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Mission Protocol: Uploading Waypoints
title: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Mission Protocol: Uploading Waypoints
description: Missions upload as MISSION_ITEMs: sequence numbers, frames (global, relative), commands, parameters — the ground station sends COUNT, the vehicle requests each item, the ground station sends them, the vehicle acks the whole set. The handshake is robust to lossy radios by design. Then MISSION_START begins execution. Verifying the uploaded mission (read it back, compare) is the professional step amateurs skip.

t: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Debugging: Wireshark Dissectors and Logs
title: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Debugging: Wireshark Dissectors and Logs
description: MAVLink debugging has purpose-built tools: Wireshark dissects MAVLink over UDP, plotting message rates and flagging CRC errors; telemetry logs (.tlog) record every message for replay. The debugging ladder is link (bytes flowing?), framing (CRC errors?), dialect (unknown message IDs?), then semantics (right messages, wrong values?). Most 'autopilot bugs' are ground-station dialect mismatches — check the lexicon first.

t: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Parameter Protocol: Tuning Over the Air
title: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Parameter Protocol: Tuning Over the Air
description: Autopilot parameters (gains, limits, modes) are read and written over MAVLink's parameter protocol: PARAM_REQUEST_LIST, PARAM_SET, PARAM_VALUE with acks. Tuning a vehicle in the field means changing parameters over the radio and watching the response — with the discipline of recording every change (who, what, old value, new value). A parameter change is a configuration change, and configuration changes are audited.

t: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Signing: MAVLink 2 Message Authentication
title: MAVLink Protocol Libraries: Signing: MAVLink 2 Message Authentication
description: MAVLink 2 signing appends a 13-byte signature (link ID, timestamp, 48-bit HMAC-SHA256-48 truncated) computed with a shared secret. It authenticates the sender and defeats replay within the timestamp window — but key distribution is the hard part, and unsigned fallback is the vulnerability. Programs that need link security use signing plus the operational discipline of key management; programs that skip it accept spoofable links knowingly.
